newsitem.title: JAPAN: FEATURE-HK handover unlikely to alter Asia security.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-HK handover unlikely to alter Asia security.

text.p: Hong Kong's return to Chinese rule is unlikely to immediately alter Asia's security balance because the British colony long ago lost its importance as a military outpost for either Beijing or Washington and its allies.

But western intelligence officials still plan to closely watch the territory, not so much to monitor military movements by China but economic ones -- particularly any moves to start military-related businesses as a means to upgrade and expand its military arsenal.
With the wealth available in Hong Kong, officials fear that if China does not stick to its pledge not to divert money from the island, the military could speed up efforts to modernise weapons.

"The business performance of the PLA (People's Liberation Army) in Hong Kong after the handover is an unknown factor but we expect it to take part in the Hong Kong economy sometime in the future," said Japanese strategic analyst Shigeo Hiramatsu.
NO THREAT SEEN TO U.S.-JAPAN ALLIANCE
Another military analyst, Kazuhisa Ogawa, said he saw no threat to the U.S.-Japan alliance, which for two decades has been the cornerstone for western defence in Asia.

With aircraft carriers, fighter jets and U.S. marine units securely stationed in bases in Japan, the United States has had no need for further advance deployment of its forces in the region, such as troops or port facilities in Hong Kong, he said.
"As long as the U.S.-Japan alliance is strong, the United States can easily commit itself to the Indian and Pacific oceans," Ogawa told Reuters.
"The idea that the United States and the West will lose Hong Kong as a strategic port of call is nonsense," Ogawa added.
Japanese navy officials agree.

"There is no dry dock for making major repairs to navy vessels," said one senior officer. "There is no reason for China to build a strategic base in Hong Kong, where it's very crowded and conspicuous."
Analysts even dismiss China's building of a modern military base on Stonecutter's Island, on the Kowloon side of Hong Kong harbour, as more for show than a strategic outpost.
CHINA HAS PLENTY OF ALTERNATE BASES
"China does not need Hong Kong as a forward base. They have enough such naval and other bases in the surrounding area anyway," said Hiramatsu.

China's South China Sea Fleet, whose area of operations include the disputed Spratly Islands in the South China Sea, is headquartered in Zhanjiang, southwest of Hong Kong, and operates bases on Hainan Island.
The troubled Taiwan Strait is covered by bases further north in Fujian Province.
Analysts say better weapons, not more bases, is what China needs for its security.

China's military is deficient in three main areas to stage full-scale amphibious operations -- naval support fire, combat aircraft and amphibious assault ships, said Naotoshi Sakonjo, research associate at Japan's Research Institute for Peace and Security.
Money and upgraded weapons are the only way to solve the shortcomings, which is why a possible military move into Hong Kong business would be so closely watched.
Aware of the concern, China has tried to damp down speculation about a so-called PLA Inc.
CHINA PLEDGES TO BAN PLA FROM BUSINESS
In April, Major General Xiong Zi Ren, political commissar of the PLA's new Hong Kong Garrison, said the PLA will be banned from taking part in the manufacturing sector.
"Some Hong Kong compatriots worry whether the garrison will respect regulations, or whether they will run businesses," Xiong told a seminar on Hong Kong's transition.
"I can categorically tell you that we resolutely will abide by all regulations set out in the law. We have already set a rule that bans involvement in production business," Xiong said.
Hiramatsu said athletic and soccer fields and a theatre inside the Stonecutter's Island base were signs that China was aware of the need to keep a friendly military profile in post-Britain Hong Kong.
"In any case, the modernisation of China's military is a long-term plan and this will not immediately affect the U.S.-dominated security picture of the region," Hiramatsu said.
